source.title: Exact results and open questions in first principle functional RG

accepted.question_text: Can one develop a unified functional renormalization-group framework for strong-disorder systems that, instead of tracking only rapidly growing disorder moments associated with rare events, follows the full probability distributions that govern typical events and works beyond the few special strong-disorder examples already understood?

evidence.quote: An outstanding question is how general this is, whether other systems can be treated in that way, and whether a unified (functional) RG approach to strong disorder problems can be found.

accepted.question_text: For pinned elastic manifolds in a glass phase, are the two sectors that dominate different observables—(i) the zero-temperature sector encoding the critical ground-state statistics of the unique ground state u1(x), and (ii) the rare low-temperature quasi-degeneracy sector that controls thermal correlations—effectively decoupled, or do they feed back strongly on each other within the field theory?

evidence.quote: As emphasized in34,36 a challenge for the field theory is to be able to describe both (i) typical events, i.e. zero temperature correlations encoding the full ground state statistics of u1(x) (believed, surely not yet proved, to be critical and universal), and (ii) significant rare events, i.e. the ones which would lead to universal behaviour in thermal correlations. An important question is whether these are two decoupled sectors or how much mutual feedback they enjoy.

accepted.question_text: How can the functional renormalization-group treatment of disordered elastic manifolds control the physics of multiple metastable minima and quasi-degenerate states in a systematic way, given that the proliferation of minima makes the problem appear intrinsically non-perturbative?

evidence.quote: It is true however that handling multiple minima intuitively appear as a non perturbative problem, so it remains to be understood precisely how it can ever be controlled.

accepted.question_text: Is the solvable large-N static limit representative of the finite-N statics of pinned manifolds, or is infinite N a peculiar limit whose behavior changes qualitatively once N is large but finite?

evidence.quote: It still remains to be understood though whether this is not a rather peculiar limit (i.e. whether large but finite N be different from infinite N).

accepted.question_text: Starting from a nonzero bare temperature for a pinned elastic manifold, how does the flow toward T_L = T L^{-θ} → 0 produce a well-defined zero-temperature critical theory with all ambiguities resolved, and how can information about the outer region R(u) for u = O(1) be matched to the derivatives of R(u) at u = 0 that require the thermal boundary layer u ∼ T_L?

evidence.quote: An outstanding question in FRG, i.e. how temperature regularizes the otherwise singular flow of T = 0 FRG, maps to the viscous layer regularization of inertial range Burgers turbulence (i.e. to the construction of the inviscid limit).

The ultimate goal is to understand how a critical theory emerges in the large system size limit L → ∞, i.e. how, starting from a non zero bare temperature, the limit TL = T L−θ → 0 can produce an asymptotic "zero temperature theory" with all ambiguities resolved. It requires solving the so-called matching problem: one wants to connect information about e.g. R(u) for u ∼ O(1) (which is what the ǫ expansion a priori computes), to derivatives of R(u) at u = 0, needed to compute correlations, which a priori requires knowledge of the function within the TBL u ∼ TL.

accepted.question_text: Can the partial-boundary-layer strategy that yields an ambiguity-free zero-temperature beta function in the d = 0 toy model be extended successfully to higher internal dimension d and to N-component manifolds, where the present attempts are still inconclusive?

evidence.quote: By considering partial boundary layers, i.e. how renormalized disorder cumulants behave when multiple points are brought within u ∼ TL, we have been able to show how to derive a beta function for the T = 0 theory. Extensions to higher d and N have been attempted but are not yet conclusive36,66.

accepted.question_text: Can the direct finite-temperature loop expansion of the functional renormalization group be reorganized or resummed in a consistent way, equivalent to the exact renormalization-group treatment, so that it remains quantitatively valid beyond the low-loop regime instead of failing in the thermal boundary layer?

evidence.quote: However, we cannot exclude that a clever way may exist to resum consistently, equivalent to what is done with the ERG.

accepted.question_text: Can the low-temperature physics in d = 0 long-range disorder always be reduced to a two-well droplet picture, or are there regimes—especially as θ approaches 0, or in many-well / replica-symmetry-breaking situations—where more than two competing minima are essential and the simple droplet approximation fails?

evidence.quote: In d = 0 and for LR disorder (i.e. when there is a glass phase) it seems fairly inescapable, although a proof would be welcome (beyond the Sinai case).

It could fail in two ways. In the first case, two wells are indeed sufficient to describe low T , and failure would then require very peculiar correlations between E2 − E1, when it is of order T , and well positions (e.g. like eigenvalue repulsion). Or, second case, more than two wells are needed. The latter may happen as θ → 0 since then we know (e.g. for a logarithmic R0(u)) that many wells are important in the low temperature phase, where some replica symmetry breaking (RSB) phenomenon takes place3.
